analysis.one_liner: Blocks providers that took COVID-19 relief funds from seizing wages, property, or selling patients' medical debt during the pandemic.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the Senate and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required hospitals, doctors, and other providers that took federal COVID-19 relief money to stop aggressive debt collection — selling debts to collectors, placing liens, wage garnishment, and credit reporting — until at least 18 months after enactment. Patients in repayment plans could pause their payments without interest or fees piling up, and debts from COVID-19 testing and treatment would get extended insurance appeal deadlines and protection from collection. Providers that broke the rules would owe damages to patients, enforceable through class actions.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who got sick or were hospitalized during the pandemic and fell behind on medical bills. The bill would have protected anyone treated by a provider that accepted federal COVID-19 relief funds — which was nearly every hospital — from having their debt sold to collection agencies, liens placed on their property, or other aggressive collection actions for at least 18 months. Patients on repayment plans could pause payments without interest or fees accruing, and people billed for COVID-19 testing or treatment got extra time to appeal insurance denials and protection from interest, fees, and collection. The bill specifically required notices in accessible language for patients with limited English proficiency.

how_it_helps.text: Covered providers and their agents would have had to suspend all extraordinary collection actions on medical debts during a covered period running at least 18 months from enactment.

Patients on repayment plans could request a suspension of payments for the covered period, with no interest or fees accruing during the suspension and reasonable forbearance options when payments resumed.

Medical debts from COVID-19 testing and treatment (February 1, 2020 onward) would be protected: extended appeal deadlines for insurance, Medicare, and Medicaid denials, no interest or fees, and no extraordinary collection actions.
Providers that violated the rules would owe patients actual damages plus up to $1,000 per violation, with class actions possible and attorney's fees available.

analysis.who_pays: Health care providers that accepted COVID-19 relief funds (and the collection agencies they sell to), who would have had to wait at least 18 months to pursue liens, debt sales, and credit reporting on patient debts, and could face class-action damages up to $2 million or 1% of net income for violations.

drawbacks.text: The suspension was temporary and tied to the public health emergency, so it deferred collection pressure rather than eliminating the underlying medical debt, and patients would eventually owe the amounts again.

Covered providers would have had to delay collections on debts during the covered period, slowing cash flow for hospitals and clinics, including practices that had already accepted COVID-19 relief funds and relied on collections revenue.

The bill created new class-action liability exposure (penalties capped at the lesser of $2 million or 1% of a provider's annual net income), which provider groups would argue invites litigation against health care entities during a crisis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections were targeted and time-limited: they applied only to providers that took federal COVID-19 relief money, only while that relief was flowing, and allowed reasonable repayment options once payments resumed, which blunts the providers' objection that indefinite collection freezes would harm their finances. The class-action penalty cap (up to $2 million or 1% of net income) limited exposure for large providers. The main honest cost is administrative and cash-flow: hospitals and collection-dependent practices would have waited longer to be paid on some debts, and some may have priced that risk elsewhere. On balance the bill was a modest, narrow intervention whose benefits to vulnerable patients outweighed those costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health committee the day it was introduced and never moved; no committee vote, no floor action, and the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Introduced February 22, 2021 by Senator Van Hollen with three Democratic cosponsors; read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was recorded for the remainder of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023, so the bill never reached the Senate floor.

The bill would have required providers accepting COVID-19 relief funds to suspend debt sales, liens, and other extraordinary collection actions until at least 18 months after enactment, and to let patients pause repayment plans without accruing interest or fees.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health care providers that accept federal COVID-19 relief funds kept full freedom to pursue extraordinary collection actions against patients; debt buyers and collection agencies kept their supply of medical debt.

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley, Sherrod Brown, and Richard Blumenthal
for.role: Original cosponsors (3 of 50 Senate Democrats and allies)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never considered or reported the bill, leaving it without a path to the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans signed on and the bill died in committee without any recorded votes.

industries.note: Providers that took federal COVID-19 relief would have been barred from selling patient debts, placing liens, and other aggressive collection actions for at least 18 months, and could face damages up to the lesser of $2 million or 1% of net income for violations. Their interest in collecting debts ran against patients during a pandemic.

industries.industry: Debt collection agencies and credit reporting
industries.note: Third-party collectors and credit bureaus would lose the flow of hospital-sold medical debt during the covered period, since covered providers could not sell debts or report through extraordinary collection channels.
